---
title: "Animated bubble chart (gapminder)"
description: "Keyframe animation: a Gapminder bubble chart flowing over year, each bubble keyed to its country, the year counting in the title, on scales frozen once across all years."
categories: [Animation]
image: figs/gapminder-poster.png
---



vellumplot animates a plot by compiling one **keyframe** per state and tweening the
frames between them. The scales are trained **once over every state and frozen**, so
the axes, the colour key and the size legend stay put while the data moves. The
animation is non-reactive: the states are fixed up front and nothing retrains.

`transition_time()` is the idiom for a continuous time like `year`: it allocates
frames in proportion to the gaps between years and never pauses or wraps, so the
bubbles glide at a constant rate. `data_id = country` tells the tween which bubble
is which: each country moves into *its own* position in the next year, whatever
order the rows come in. The title is a template, and `{round(frame_time)}` is
evaluated on every frame, so the year counts up between keyframes in step with the
bubbles.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(gapminder)

a <- vplot(transform(gapminder, pop = pop / 1e6), width = 7, height = 4.5) |>
  mark_point(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent,
             data_id = country, alpha = 0.8) |>
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") |>
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}", x = "GDP per capita",
       y = "Life expectancy", size = "population (millions)") |>
  transition_time(year) |>
  animate(nframes = 120, fps = 20)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
anim_save("gapminder.svg", a)
```
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/gapminder.svg){width=100%}
:::
:::


Each bubble's position and size interpolate frame to frame. Because the x, y and size
scales were frozen over the union of all years, a country that is poor early and rich
late keeps one stable frame of reference throughout: China and India, the two large
green bubbles, climb from the bottom left while the axes stay where they are.

## Why SVG here

`anim_save()` picks the format from the extension. This page uses `.svg`, which writes
every frame as vector markup in a single file, stepped by CSS: crisp at any zoom, text
that stays text, and a first frame held still for readers whose system asks for reduced
motion.

An animated SVG grows with marks times frames, and 142 bubbles over 120 frames is
about 3 MB on disk. But SVG is text, and web servers compress it: this file travels as
under 200 KB, where the same animation as an animated PNG (`.png`) is about 5.5 MB
and does not compress further. A raster format wins when a scene is truly dense (thousands
of marks a frame, or a datashaded field); for a few hundred moving shapes, vector is
the better trade. [An animation with no pixels in it](animated-svg.qmd) covers the
format in more detail.
